name: Preservation rhinoplasty

card.summary: Nose surgery that lowers or reshapes the bridge while keeping the natural dorsal structure intact rather than cutting a hump off; popular among surgeons, with mostly case-series evidence.
card.aka: Dorsal preservation rhinoplasty, push-down / let-down technique
card.note: Hump recurrence and technique-specific problems are discussed in the literature; evidence is largely retrospective.

quick.overview:
Preservation rhinoplasty is an approach in which the surgeon keeps the nose's original bony and cartilaginous bridge and lowers it as a unit, instead of the traditional method of cutting off a dorsal hump. The term was coined by Daniel in 2018, according to a case-series paper.
Surgical authors describe it as a shift in philosophy, with claims of better aesthetic and functional results that are still being tested.
quick.mechanism: The osseocartilaginous vault is mobilised as a single unit and pushed down or let down (push-down and let-down techniques), preserving natural dorsal lines and mucosa. Several classification systems and hybrid approaches have been proposed.
quick.risks: Reported problems include hump recurrence after let-down or push-down surgery. The evidence comprises retrospective series, a radiological comparison with hump resection, and registered trials.

lead: Preservation rhinoplasty, also called dorsal preservation rhinoplasty, refers to techniques that address a dorsal hump or the nasal profile by repositioning rather than removing the natural dorsum. A 2020 review notes a rekindled interest in dorsal preservation as an alternative to conventional hump resection, with claims of superior functional and aesthetic results, and describes mobilising the osseocartilaginous vault as a single unit to avoid disrupting natural structure.[1]

A 2018 article titled as a rhinoplasty revolution popularised the term, and a 2020 case series states that the term was coined by Daniel in 2018 and represents a fundamental change in philosophy.[2][3] Later papers proposed classification systems, hybrid structural approaches and guidelines.[4][5][6]
The evidence base consists mainly of retrospective series and comparisons, alongside two small randomised trials published in 2024.
infobox: Push-down, let-down, cartilage conversion, hybrid osteoplasty

paras: Conventional hump reduction cuts the cartilage of the hump with a scalpel and chisels the bone with an osteotome, then smooths the result with rasps.[21] Preservation approaches instead lower the hump by reshaping the structures beneath it and keeping the roof of the nose intact, so the natural dorsal contour is retained rather than rebuilt.[1]

A review of the Brazilian approach reports that surgeons in Brazil began using dorsal preservation in the 1970s, that indications were gradually expanded to almost every kind of nose, and that power tools such as piezoelectric devices and drills later refined execution; it states that the techniques are now adopted by many surgeons worldwide.[18]

Reviews describe further developments: bony dorsal preservation, aimed at crooked noses, lowers humps without creating an open roof deformity,[16] and subdorsal cantilever grafts let surgeons augment the dorsum while using preservation concepts.[17] A review of male rhinoplasty notes that fewer men than women seek the surgery, that body dysmorphic syndrome is reported at a higher rate in men presenting for rhinoplasty, and that consultation should be thorough.[15]

Push-down and let-down are two main variants; one study used push-down for humps under 4 mm and let-down for larger ones.[7] A practical classification system, guidelines for primary rhinoplasty and a structural hybrid approach have been published, as have techniques converting cartilage to expand indications.[4][5][6][8][9]

A 100-case series with one-year follow-up reported on decision making in preservation rhinoplasty.[3] A study of 520 patients discussed reasons for dorsal hump recurrence after let-down or push-down surgery and proposed solutions.[7] A radiological study compared the effect on the internal nasal valve of dorsal preservation versus hump resection.[10] A review of current trends summarises the field.[11]

Human data are largely retrospective: a 153-patient primary series (100 with one-year follow-up), a 520-patient series on hump relapse, and a quantitative radiological comparison with hump resection.[3][7][10] Registered trials include a completed study of nasal valve angle and area (100 patients) and an active trial of hybrid osteoplasty versus osteotomy (200 patients).[12][13]

Two randomised trials published in 2024 compared dorsal preservation with conventional approaches: a prospective double-blinded trial of 50 patients compared it with hump reduction using patient-reported outcomes and cone-beam CT,[19] and a trial of 84 patients compared it with hump resection plus spreader-flap reconstruction on functional and aesthetic outcomes.[20] Published abstracts available here do not state the numerical findings, so they are not summarised.

A published discussion among surgeons on controversies in preservation rhinoplasty features Joao Carlos Neves recounting how the techniques evolved, Dean Toriumi describing a cautious start in 2019 followed by expansion to more varied nasal deformities, and Ali Goksel stressing surgical expertise and individual assessment; techniques such as dorsum-plasty osteotomies and the Ballerina maneuver are discussed for improving results.[14]

timeline.event: Term preservation rhinoplasty coined and article on a rhinoplasty revolution published.[2][3]
Review and modification of dorsal preservation techniques; 100-case series reported.[1][3]
Practical classification system and guidelines for dorsum preservation published.[4][5]
Brazilian surgeons begin using dorsal preservation rhinoplasty.[18]
The term preservation rhinoplasty is popularised and said to be coined by Daniel.[2][3]
Randomised trials compare dorsal preservation with hump reduction.[19][20]
